cards.text: The heart's two pumps feed two circuits in {{c1::series}}, not in parallel: all blood leaving one passes through the other before completing the loop.
Venous blood reaches the right atrium through three doors: the {{c1::superior vena cava}}, the {{c2::inferior vena cava}}, and the {{c3::coronary sinus}}.
cards.extra: Coronary sinus brings the heart muscle's own blood.

cards.text: The coronary arteries arise from the {{c1::aortic root}}, just above the aortic valve, so the heart is the first territory the aorta supplies.

The three fetal shunts are the {{c1::ductus venosus}} (placenta → IVC, bypassing liver), the {{c2::foramen ovale}} (RA → LA, bypassing lung), and the {{c3::ductus arteriosus}} (pulmonary trunk → aorta).
cards.extra: In the fetus the placenta oxygenates the blood, not the lung.

cards.text: After birth the ductus venosus becomes the {{c1::ligamentum venosum}}, the foramen ovale becomes the {{c2::fossa ovalis}}, and the ductus arteriosus becomes the {{c3::ligamentum arteriosum}}.
cards.extra: First breath drops pulmonary pressure; the shunts close into fibrous scars.

cards.text: The ascending aorta gives only two branches, the {{c1::coronaries}}; then come the arch, thoracic and abdominal aorta, and the bifurcation into the {{c2::common iliac}} arteries.
Organizing principle of the arterial tree: each artery is named by the {{c1::territory it serves}} (renal → kidney, hepatic → liver, splenic → spleen).
cards.extra: A map of territories, not rote names.

cards.text: The aortic arch gives three branches: the {{c1::brachiocephalic trunk}} (splitting into right common carotid + right subclavian), the left common carotid, and the left subclavian.
cards.extra: Right = one trunk that splits; left = vessels arise separately.

cards.text: On the way to the upper limb, the subclavian artery becomes the {{c1::axillary}}, then {{c2::brachial}}, then {{c3::radial and ulnar}} in the forearm.
The brain is supplied by two sources, the {{c1::internal carotids}} (front) and the {{c2::vertebral}} arteries (back), which unite in the {{c3::circle of Willis}}.
cards.extra: The ring is an anastomosis: if one source occludes, blood arrives via the other.

cards.text: Aortic branches split into {{c1::visceral}} (to organs: bronchial, esophageal, pericardial) and {{c2::parietal}} (to the wall: posterior intercostal, superior phrenic).
cards.extra: Same viscera-vs-wall key in thorax and abdomen.

cards.text: The three unpaired visceral branches of the abdominal aorta feed the gut: {{c1::celiac trunk}} (liver, stomach, spleen), {{c2::superior mesenteric}} (small bowel + right colon), and {{c3::inferior mesenteric}} (left colon + rectum).
cards.extra: This territory's returning blood is what detours through the liver.

cards.text: The paired branches of the abdominal aorta, arising laterally to bilateral organs, are the {{c1::suprarenal, renal, and gonadal}} arteries.
The aorta bifurcates into common iliacs; each splits into the {{c1::external}} iliac (→ femoral, lower limb) and the {{c2::internal}} iliac (pelvic organs).
Limb veins have three layers: {{c1::deep}} (with the arteries), {{c2::superficial}} (great and small saphenous), and {{c3::perforating}} (pierce the fascia, linking superficial to deep).
cards.extra: Perforator valves drive blood from superficial to deep.

cards.text: When perforating-vein valves fail, blood refluxes and pools in the superficial veins, which swell and become tortuous: {{c1::varicose veins}}.
In the hepatic portal system the mesenteric and splenic veins form the {{c1::portal vein}}, which enters the liver before blood goes on via the hepatic veins to the IVC.
cards.extra: Gut blood is inspected by the liver before general circulation.

cards.text: What makes the portal system special is that blood crosses {{c1::two capillary beds in series}}: the gut, then the liver.
The {{c1::azygos}} system, ascending along the spine into the SVC, acts as a collateral bridge between the two {{c2::venae cavae}}.
cards.extra: Venous version of the circle-of-Willis idea; rescue route when a cava occludes.

cards.text: Obstruction of the superior vena cava (e.g., mediastinal tumor) causes {{c1::SVC syndrome}}: congested face and neck with dilated collateral chest veins.
cards.extra: The visible dilated veins are the azygos rescue in action.
